papers.title: Factor Rank: A Canonical Algebraic Generalization of Tree Decision Diagrams
papers.summary: Tree decision diagrams (TDDs), recently introduced by Capelli et al. (SAT 2026), are representations of Boolean functions. They generalize OBDDs by replacing variable orders with vtrees. The width of a TDD counts the distinct subfunctions across each vtree cut. Counting subfunctions is blind to linear structure. We introduce algebraic tree decision diagrams (ATDDs) by replacing this count with the rank of the cut matrix. The maximum of these ranks over all cuts, the factor rank, is exactly the width of the ATDD. Every TDD can be converted into an ATDD of no greater width. An ATDD is a tree tensor network in canonical form. ATDDs are exponentially more succinct than TDDs, and quasi-polynomially more succinct than structured deterministic DNNFs. Our main result is that this gain in succinctness does not cost canonicity. ATDDs are the first strict canonical form for a rank-based representation over arbitrary vtrees. For each function and vtree there is exactly one ATDD, over the rationals and without any genericity assumption. The canonicity admits a local characterization. Whether a tree tensor network is the ATDD of the Boolean function it computes can be checked in polynomial time from its tensors alone. Equivalence checking becomes a test of syntactic equality. The operation set includes polynomial-time model counting, weighted model counting, and a test whether a tree tensor network represents a Boolean function. Capelli et al. asked for the complexity of changing the vtree of a TDD and suggested local vtree changes. We answer the question. After a rotation of the vtree at one node, the new ATDD differs from the old one in two tensors only. Vtree change runs in output-polynomial time both for TDDs and for ATDDs. We formalize and verify our core results in Lean. We provide a prototype implementation of TDD and ATDD compilers as a first empirical validation.

papers.title: CompAIssionate Other: Identity Assumptions in LLM Responses to Distress
papers.summary: Individuals experiencing suicidal ideation (SI) or psychological distress may disclose their social identities when seeking support from LLMs. Attending to identity-related stressors can be important for providing contextually appropriate and empathetic support. However, disclosing an identity does not necessarily mean that it is a cause of distress. In this work, we audit how LLMs interpret distress through disclosed identities. Using paired counterfactual interventions, we evaluate six LLMs across two SI and distress datasets, 16 identity and control conditions, and two prompting protocols. Our findings suggest that models can transform identity disclosures into explanatory narratives, attributing distress to presumed identity-related adversity. These assumptions frequently appear within otherwise empathetic responses, particularly when marginalized identities are disclosed. We contextualize our findings through the lens of compassionate othering to characterize these patterns as a form of harm in which empathetic responses impose identity-linked assumptions on individual suffering. These responses can misrepresent individuals' experiences by treating their identities as explanations for distress without supporting evidence. Our findings highlight the need to mitigate these harms by grounding interpretations of distress in individuals' disclosures and avoiding unsupported identity-linked assumptions.

papers.title: Token Inflation: How Dishonest Providers Can Overcharge for Large Language Model Usage
papers.summary: Per-token billing is now the standard pricing model for commercial large language models (LLMs), so the honesty of reported token counts directly affects what users pay. We show that this kind of billing is hard to audit by design: providers hide the model, the tokenizer, and the execution to protect their IP, mitigate jailbreaks, and preserve user privacy, which means an auditor can only inspect proofs the provider supplies. The audit therefore reduces to a consistency check on the provider's own reports. We call this a trust paradox: every audit must trust some artifact, but current frameworks trust exactly the ones a provider has the strongest reason to manipulate. We study three recent token auditing frameworks and show that a provider with ordinary commercial capabilities can systematically inflate billed token counts. In the most permissive setting, hidden reasoning usage can be inflated by 1,469% on average without detection. At current frontier reasoning prices, that turns a \$100 honest bill into roughly a \$1,569 bill on the same query. Even when the user can see the full reasoning string, tokenization ambiguity alone still allows 50.85% over-reporting below the detection threshold. These results suggest the problem is not in any specific auditor but in any audit whose evidence comes from the audited party. Restoring honest billing will require verification that ties reported token counts to evidence the provider does not control, such as trusted execution attestation, cryptographic proofs of inference, or third-party re-execution.

papers.title: Trustworthy Recursive Self-Improvement with Statistical Guarantees
papers.summary: Recursive self-improvement offers a promising path toward AI agents that improve through experience by refining their own harnesses without retraining their underlying large language models (LLMs). Making this self-improvement process reliable, however, requires more than generating new updates: agents must decide which changes are worth keeping. A greedy gate that accepts updates based solely on higher validation scores can mistake an observed gain for genuine progress and lead to performance degeneration, whereas overly conservative statistical gates may reject beneficial updates and hinder performance improvement. We introduce Trustworthy Recursive Updates with Statistical Testing (TRUST), a framework that adapts an online multiple hypothesis testing procedure to control the rate of false evolution across rounds, with an LLM analyzing historical context to help determine how much evidence is required to update the incumbent. Under interpretable assumptions, we prove that TRUST limits the proportion of accepted updates that result in unacceptable performance loss. We further derive a lower bound on the final performance gain. Across the benchmarks HotpotQA, DROP, and APPS with the models DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen-3.8-Flash, TRUST reduces the average ratio of accepted inferior updates from the greedy gate's 45.59% to 2.78%, while achieving higher final scores than the state-of-the-art statistical gate baselines for recursive self-improvement. These findings demonstrate that TRUST strikes a balance between statistical reliability and performance gain in recursive self-improvement.

papers.title: Proximal Preference Optimization: A Unified Framework for Stable and Reward-Free Alignment
papers.summary: We introduce a proximal preference optimization framework that unifies the implicit reward formulation of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) with the trust-region stability of Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). papers.title: Rank-Aware Spectral Bounds on Attention Logits for Stable Low-Precision Training

papers.title: Interpreting Neural Combinatorial Optimization via Evolving Programmatic Bottlenecks
papers.summary: While Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) achieves strong performance, its interpretability remains an open question. A natural surrogate is a Concept Bottleneck Model (CBM), yet standard concepts are input attributes, whereas NCO is better explained by decision rules that are hard to predefine. EPB thus uses LLMs to evolve a bank of programmatic decision rules as concepts, each producing an action distribution, where a learned state-dependent router then mixes them to form the surrogate action. We optimize EPB through an iterative framework: Block I fixes the bank size and introduces the hybrid textual-numerical gradient descent to jointly optimize the textual programs and the numerical router; Block II adapts the bank size via failure-targeted expansion and redundancy pruning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the EPB surrogate closely matches the teacher's behavior and solution quality. We then analyze the distilled rules, reveal several NCO decision patterns, and verify the rules' faithfulness to the surrogate's decisions. Moreover, the surrogate allows targeted program edits that improve its generalization beyond the teacher. Our work advances interpretable NCO and establishes EPB as a promising direction for interpreting complex learned decision-making policies.

papers.title: BAPLe++: Cross-Model Transferability and Prompt-Level Defense of Backdoors in Medical Foundation Models

papers.title: Mirage: Provable Defense Against LLM KV Cache Timing Side Channels with Topology-Aware Isolation
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as shared multi-tenant services, relying on advanced optimizations like KV cache and prefix sharing to improve throughput and reduce latency. Instead of stalling the GPU or forcing redundant recomputations, Mirage delays token emission at the gateway so the attacker observes a natural cache miss distribution, while the GPU seamlessly continues serving other requests at full speed. Mirage uses a Privacy Odometer that persistently tracks the topological novelty of prefix fan-out expansions to distinguish aggressive probing from benign traffic. Once a prefix exceeds a safety threshold, Mirage engages a two-phase policy that uses a dynamic estimator to pad the TTFT to a calibrated cache-miss baseline. On a 500-sample public corpus across three models, Mirage suppresses the timing side-channel to near the random-guessing floor, while maintaining a significantly lower TTFT than defense baselines. papers.title: The Lagrangian Brain: A Constraint Mechanics of Mind and Machine
papers.summary: A brain is in one state at a time, yet most of what decides its next state is absent from it: the patterns its world never produces, the statistics of a lifetime, a goal that lies ahead. In mechanics a wire acts on a bead only through a force that appears when the bead presses on it, and Lagrange computed such forces with one multiplier for each constraint. We propose that a brain follows the same mechanics. Everything a circuit knows, is told or wants is a constraint on its single state and acts through its own multiplier, which accumulates the violation and pushes the state back. Neurons and synapses carry the multipliers, each with its own time constant: inhibitory interneurons carry what never happens, adaptation the cost of staying in one state, synapses the statistics of experience, and feedback to apical dendrites the future. From this hypothesis follow Dale's law, the reciprocal wiring and balance of excitation and inhibition, the paradoxical responses of cortex and the frequencies of brain rhythms. Belief becomes the time one trajectory spends in each state, learning becomes sleep proposing laws and waking refuting the false ones, and planning becomes a wave from the goal meeting a wave from the present. Connectionism and symbolism are the limits of frozen and of instantaneous multipliers, and between them the time a circuit runs becomes the depth of its computation. A machine built on these principles, trained without gradients on 1000 solved puzzles, solves all 422,786 Sudoku-Extreme test puzzles with one trajectory each. It rediscovers the rules of Sudoku by sleeping and waking, plans shortest paths in mazes of 64 times the training area, and tracks permutations exactly on strings 25 times longer than in training, where Transformers fail. A mind, on this view, is life that learns its own constraints.

papers.title: No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?
papers.summary: Pre-training is where every foundation model begins; bringing recursive self-improvement (RSI) there would let AI improve the process that creates AI. papers.title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
papers.summary: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model. Two common approaches to rank-specific extraction are direct rank truncation and Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of the dense update. Direct prefix truncation keeps the leading columns of one aggregated factor and the corresponding rows of the other. It is cheap but can increase reconstruction error. The dense SVD approach first forms the product of aggregated LoRA factors. It then decomposes this matrix and retains the leading singular components to construct adapters at the target rank. This gives the optimal rank-constrained approximation in Frobenius norm but incurs significant computational overhead. To address this trade-off, we propose RBLA+ as an extension of RBLA. It uses established compact QR/core-SVD decomposition to minimize Frobenius error for the extracted LoRA update without forming the dense update. It also accounts for client and server scaling conventions during upload and broadcast. Across vision and language tasks, RBLA+ improves accuracy over RBLA in multiple heterogeneous settings. In CPU benchmarks with synthetic adapters, RBLA+ has lower extraction time than the dense partial-SVD baseline. RBLA+ preserves each client's prescribed adapter size and per-round communication payload.

papers.title: Spectral Feedback for Test-Time Alignment of Protein Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Discrete diffusion models have become leading architectures for inverse protein folding. Test-time alignment guides these models during inference to generate proteins with desirable attributes. Alignment methods for discrete diffusion models often treat inference as a unidirectional process, lacking effective mechanisms for revisiting undesirable token selections. We introduce Spectral Feedback, an algorithm that selects edit-positions in a feedback loop, allowing the model to iteratively correct its own generations. This approach leverages the masking structure of discrete diffusion models by re-masking and re-sampling tokens. While prior alignment methods focus on what token labels to assign to maximize a target reward, we instead treat which tokens to revisit as the central alignment problem. Selecting edit-positions is challenging because edit effects are interdependent: the impact of modifying one token depends on which others are edited simultaneously. We define an edit-set as a set of positions to edit by re-masking and re-sampling the corresponding tokens in a sequence. Motivated by prior work on sparse interactions in biological systems, we find empirically that edit-set value functions for protein inverse folding admit sparse Fourier representations. This structure enables Spectral Feedback to efficiently learn and optimize the value functions for edit-position selection. Spectral Feedback is model-agnostic and can be applied to pre-trained, test-time aligned, and fine-tuned diffusion models without modifying the underlying generative processes. Applied to inverse folding with a protein stability reward oracle, Spectral Feedback increases the proportion of stable proteins by 32.3 percentage points over a pre-trained model, 24.8 over Best-of-10, and 5.8 over a state-of-the-art RL fine-tuned diffusion model.

papers.title: Reason First, Retrieve What Matters: Hypothesis-Guided Keyframe Selection for Long Video Understanding

papers.title: AI in the Clinical Documentation Loop: Effects of LLM-Induced Note Bloat and Diagnostic Overcall on Downstream LLMs
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to process medical records for healthcare tasks such as clinical documentation. Second, injected overcalls reappeared in downstream outputs at rates that varied by reader model, without detectable changes in standard quality metrics. papers.title: Effective Unbounded Drift Control in Heterogeneous Federated Learning: Bayesian Fine-Tuning Using a Reference Model
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients while preserving data privacy. However, data and system heterogeneity often induce unbounded drift in model updates due to each clients' different multiple local steps, partial participation, and unbounded dynamics in model updates. These challenges severely degrade predictive performance, exacerbate catastrophic forgetting, and hinder global optimization forward to optimal updates. Related works (AdaBest, FedEve, A-FedPD) defined dual drift problems and proposed each regularization term to client optimization process. However, in aspect of temporal unbounded drift, they generally reflect last round temporal drift to client optimization while forgets prior temporal unbounded drift. To address these limitations, we propose FedRef, a robust optimization framework that leverages a reference model generalized from prior global models via Bayesian fine-tuning. FedRef integrates a Maximum A Posteriori (MAP)-based regularization mechanism that calibrates global updates toward a temporally aggregated reference model, thereby effectively controlling unbounded drift and maximizing empirical stability. Moreover, unlike prior approaches that rely on complex client-side optimization heuristics, FedRef achieves superior generalization to reflect recency weighting by seamlessly blending a robust probabilistic prior with global likelihood optimization. By maintaining a temporal moving average centered on previous global trajectories, the proposed framework provides a highly reliable optimization anchor.

papers.title: Large Language Models without QK-Normalization
papers.summary: Query-Key Normalization (QK-Norm) is widely adopted in modern large language models to control the growth of attention logits and improve training stability. However, query and key norms are not merely sources of instability. Rather than removing magnitude through normalization, QK-MAP transforms the input representation using multiple learnable frequencies, so that changes in magnitude are encoded as bounded phase patterns. This allows magnitude to be represented through phase and direction rather than vector length alone. Its periodic features have a fixed norm while remaining sensitive to magnitude changes, separating magnitude encoding from norm growth. Multiple frequencies further help distinguish magnitudes and reduce periodic ambiguity. Experiments across model scales from 190M to 7B parameters show that QK-MAP achieves lower training and validation loss than both Standard attention and QK-Norm. Further analyses show that QK-MAP preserves sensitivity to input scale, assigns less attention to the first token, and produces stronger attention contrast for relevant evidence in synthetic long-context tests. These results demonstrate that query-key scale can be effectively controlled without sacrificing token-specific magnitude information.

papers.title: Parallel Rollout Approximation for Pixel-Space Autoregressive Image Generation
papers.summary: Pixel-space continuous-token autoregressive (AR) generation directly models images as sequences of raw pixel patches, avoiding discrete tokenization or a separately pretrained tokenizer. papers.title: Sparsity and Out-of-Distribution Generalization
papers.summary: Explaining out-of-distribution generalization has been a central problem in epistemology since Goodman's "grue" puzzle in 1946. Today it's a central problem in machine learning, including AI alignment. Here we propose a principled account of OOD generalization with three main ingredients. First, the world is always presented to experience not as an amorphous mass, but via distinguished features (for example, visual and auditory channels). Second, Occam's Razor favors hypotheses that are "sparse," meaning that they depend on as few features as possible. Third, sparse hypotheses will generalize from a training to a test distribution, provided the two distributions sufficiently overlap on their restrictions to the features that are either actually relevant or hypothesized to be. The two distributions could diverge arbitrarily on other features. We prove a simple theorem that formalizes the above intuitions, generalizing the classic sample complexity bound of Blumer et al. to an OOD context. We then generalize sparse classifiers to subspace juntas, where the ground truth classifier depends solely on a low-dimensional linear subspace of the features.

papers.title: Predictive Surprise as Self-Grounding Concept Bottleneck for Interpretable Time Series
papers.summary: Time-series classifiers deployed in risk-sensitive domains must be (1) accurate, (2) interpretable, and (3) able to abstain when evidence is weak. Existing methods do not deliver all 3 at once, and the obstacle is structural, rather than logistical. Meaningful temporal patterns cannot be defined without knowing segment boundaries, yet meaningful boundaries cannot be placed without knowing which patterns to expect. Existing approaches break this circularity by using fixed windows or expert-annotated vocabularies, thereby sacrificing at least one of the 3 properties. We introduce ConceptTime, which closes the loop through a single self-supervised signal. A frozen probabilistic forecaster predicts a distribution over the next observation at every timestep of the sequence. We call the mismatch between its prediction and the realized signal the predictive surprise. This signal both locates segment boundaries and characterizes each resulting segment through the forecaster. Segments are thus grounded by how they behaved relative to expectation, not by what they look like. These summaries cluster into a vocabulary of dynamical regimes that we call concepts. A lightweight head classifies from the concept sequence, and the distance to the nearest concept yields reliability by design. Across 17 public benchmarks, ConceptTime is competitive with state-of-the-art black-box accuracy, beats every interpretable baseline, and retains near-98% accuracy on Epilepsy with 1% of labels. It further remains competitive with softmax, prototype-distance, and SHAP/TimeX/TimeX++ on OOD detection and deletion faithfulness, without a single annotation, language model call, or domain expert. papers.title: Sampling Is Not Curiosity: Why LLM Agents Should Investigate
papers.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended tasks, very common in research scenarios where they are required to explore, investigate, or act curiously. At inference time, an LLM is a fixed map from context to next-token distribution, the pretrained weights determine the function, and only its conditioning changes as context accumulates. Mechanisms like temperature, best-of-N, tree search, or RAG vary how the distribution is sampled or what it is conditioned on, but do not update the agent's model of the environment. We argue that current LLM agents do not explore curiously; they explore stochastically. From how curiosity is understood in the RL literature, it requires a predictive structure over how the environment responds to the agent's actions, which improves online from current interaction, drives action selection through its predicted improvement, and persists beyond the context window. Additionally, in its open-ended form, the agent should intrinsically originate what to investigate. Thus, we propose a framework defining curiosity in LLM agents, reserving the term for systems that satisfy it. In doing so, we identify the research directions its implementation opens up.

papers.title: Subliminal Learning Is Steering Vector Distillation
papers.summary: Subliminal learning refers to a student language model acquiring a teacher's traits (e.g. a system-prompted preference for owls) when fine-tuned on the teacher's outputs, despite the outputs being semantically unrelated to those traits. System prompts that are not well approximated by steering vectors are not subliminally learned. This is a special case of steering vector distillation, in which a student trained on the outputs of a steered teacher learns to imitate that steering. We demonstrate steering vector distillation on a range of semantic and random vectors. Adding a semantic vector to a model's activations can have both model-independent and model-specific (i.e. non-semantic) effects on its behavior, so generated data that is non-semantic can transmit a vector with semantic effects, enabling subliminal learning. This also explains why subliminal learning does not transfer between models. We find that adaptive optimizers are necessary for subliminal learning in language models: activation gradients on steered data carry a small but consistent component along the steering direction, and non-adaptive optimizers impede this by allowing outlier gradients to dominate.

papers.title: MARR: Module-Adaptive Residual Reconstruction for Low-Bit Post-Training Quantization
papers.summary: Recently, residual reconstruction-based model quantization methods have achieved promising performance in low-bit Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) by introducing cross-module residuals to reduce error accumulated from previous modules. Therefore, in this work, we propose a residual regulation strategy to mitigate the HA bias associated with residual strength, while preserving accumulated-error correction. Furthermore, we observe that this two-sided effect is module-dependent, we futher propose a Module-Adaptive Residual Reconstruction (MARR), which assigns a module-specific scaling coefficient to adaptively balance accumulated-error correction and residual-related HA bias for each module. To avoid exhaustive per-module coefficient search and obtain a stable coefficient estimate, we design an Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID)-based update strategy that employs reconstruction error as feedback to progressively refine this coefficient. papers.title: Test-time scaling of diffusions with flow maps
papers.summary: A common recipe to improve diffusion models at test-time so that samples score highly against a user-specified reward is to introduce the gradient of the reward into the dynamics of the diffusion itself. papers.title: Do Semantic Distance Tests Actually Predict Creativity in LLMs? Evidence for Jagged Creativity
papers.summary: Measuring the creativity of large language models (LLMs) is essential for designing methods that can improve creativity and for enhancing our scientific understanding of this ability. (2) The Remote Associates Test is effectively a proxy for general capabilities rather than a specific predictor of creativity in LLMs. (3) Lastly, the Divergent Association Task is the best predictor of creative writing, but no single test predicts all constructs well. In summary, our results prescribe caution when applying psychometric tests and tasks of creativity validated among human populations to LLMs.

papers.title: HexIt: Learning Hexahedral Block Decomposition with Expert Iteration on Combinatorial Maps

papers.title: Beyond Query Similarity: Safety-Conditioned Cache Routing for LLM Response Reuse

papers.title: Mechanistic Interpretability with Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators

papers.title: Language-Based Agent Control

papers.title: Shifting the Gradient: Understanding How Defensive Training Methods Protect Language Model Integrity

papers.title: What Can Analogy Tell Us About Artificial Consciousness?
papers.summary: Who or what is conscious? Because subjective experience is directly accessible only in the first person, judgments about consciousness in other entities depend partly on analogy. papers.title: Update Slope Is Bounded by Prior Calibration: A Structural Bound and Its Contingent Empirical Signature

papers.title: Governing Well in the Algorithmic Age: The Foundations of Digital Statecraft
authors: David Uriel Socol de la Osa
papers.summary: The digital substrate - data, algorithms, infrastructure, platforms, applications - is being governed without adequate conceptual foundations. papers.summary: The development of tabular foundation models (TFMs) has accelerated in recent years, outperforming traditional ML methods on many tabular benchmarks. A key finding is that TFMs can be pretrained entirely on synthetic datasets, opening opportunities to design data generators that encourage desirable model properties. Prior work has mainly focused on crafting high-quality priors over generators to improve overall pretraining performance. Our key insight is that parameterizing the generator distribution enables an adversarial, distributional robustness perspective: during training, we can adapt the generator to emphasize datasets that are particularly challenging for the model, which we formalize by introducing an optimality gap measure. Further, we develop a method to align the synthetic data generation with real-world datasets from a given domain, constraining the adversary to generate realistic data. Together, these algorithms comprise the Robust and Domain-Adapted Tabular Foundation Models (RAD-TFM) pipeline, a model-agnostic adversarial training framework. Applied to the TabPFN V2 classifier, RAD-TFM improves performance across 6 diverse tabular benchmarks, with up to a 10.8 percentage-point improvement in mean normalized AUC over the strongest baseline, using fewer than 100k additional synthetic training datasets, less than 0.1% of the original pretraining data. Applying the same pipeline to TabICL V2 also improves performance across three major benchmarks, demonstrating the generality of the framework. These results highlight a promising new direction for targeted adversarial continued training of TFMs using synthetic data alone.

papers.title: A Continual Validation, Updating, and Decision-Making Framework for Self-Adaptive Digital Twins: A Case Study in Additive Manufacturing
papers.summary: Digital Twins support real-time decision-making through predictive models of physical systems, yet their reliability can deteriorate as operating conditions evolve. The framework is evaluated using a stochastic dynamical system with abrupt changes and a simulated directed energy deposition process with gradual changes in material properties. Results show improvements in predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation during the evaluated post-adaptation intervals, alongside improved reference tracking and reduced constraint violations in the manufacturing case study compared with the investigated baselines. These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating continual validation with model adaptation while acknowledging the trade-off between responsiveness and predictive reliability in evolving Digital Twins.

papers.title: BioBlobs: Unsupervised Discovery of Functional Substructures
papers.summary: Protein function is often localized to cohesive substructures, such as catalytic triads, binding pockets, and structural motifs, that occupy only a small fraction of a protein's residues. Yet existing predictive pipelines typically aggregate residue-level embeddings and do not explicitly model or infer these functional substructures, leaving the central biological question unanswered: which substructure of a protein is responsible for its function? Across diverse protein function prediction tasks and both sequence-only and structure-aware protein language models, BioBlobs is competitive with strong baselines while operating on only a small fraction of residues. Trained only on protein function labels, BioBlobs recovers expert-curated functional sites in InterPro and experimentally annotated catalytic sites in the Mechanism and Catalytic Site Atlas, demonstrating unsupervised functional substructure discovery and opening a path to large-scale functional site discovery in unannotated proteins. The discovered blobs adapt their spatial scale to the task, ranging from local catalytic sites to entire structural domains. Code is available at https://github.com/OliverLaboratory/BioBlobs.

papers.title: Rethinking On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
papers.summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to recursive self-improvement. In this setting, a model acts as its own teacher when augmented with privileged information, such as a solution to a math problem. Thinking models seem especially well positioned to teach themselves this way, since they can deliberate, verify, and self-correct. Surprisingly, we show that OPSD degrades thinking models on long reasoning traces: across five Qwen3 and OLMo thinking models evaluated on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25, privileged-context distillation causes a relative drop of up to 17\% in avg@16 accuracy. The degradation scales with the amount of privileged context withheld from the student and is most pronounced at long rollout budgets, where thinking models otherwise obtain their largest gains. This failure mode extends to distillation from a larger, privileged teacher: on-policy distillation (OPD) improves thinking models, but privileged OPD reverses these gains. Our diagnostics suggest that privileged teacher context reshapes learning at high-entropy forking positions, i.e., rollout positions where multiple continuations remain plausible and may lead to different reasoning paths. Privileged context lowers fork rates in thinking-model rollouts but not in instruction-tuned model rollouts, which may explain the observation that OPSD training helps instruct models more reliably than thinking models.At self-correction branches, privileged OPD penalizes sampled reconsideration tokens that vanilla OPD supports. Consistent with this, thinking models trained with a privileged teacher produce fewer verification, backtracking, and hedging markers, even after length normalization. These findings indicate that applying self-distillation methods to strong thinking models requires further consideration of token-level signal---especially around tokens related to correction and crucial reasoning steps.

papers.title: Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction
papers.summary: As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: \emph{why} should humans keep doing science, and \emph{how} should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is \emph{durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values}. From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, \emph{human understanding}, requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, \emph{human direction}, requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI's current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction.

papers.title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. papers.title: Game-Creation-Agents: Autonomous Game Production
papers.summary: Game-Creation-Agents (GCA) turns a natural-language request into a runnable Phaser 4 browser game. The pipeline first builds a multimodal game design document that couples mechanics and scene contracts to grounded visual references. Build-linked real-UI checks and a code-blind critic then verify that build and decide whether the game may ship. Each blocker returns to the agent that owns the affected artifact for a bounded repair, and the game is released once all the gates pass. papers.title: Generative Active Learning for Label-Efficient Pan-Organ Ultrasound Diagnosis

papers.title: Does Your Neural Network Extrapolate? Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization
papers.summary: Deep neural networks can learn salient features from an in-distribution (ID) training window without identifying the data-generating structure needed for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. Understanding this limitation requires examining the identifiability of the data-generating process (DGP). From a single training window, the DGP that yields the correct OOD extrapolation is not identifiable: infinitely many DGPs are observationally equivalent within a fixed tolerance on that window yet diverge arbitrarily beyond it, and no ID criterion alone can reliably distinguish them. A structural commitment---the feature map, label map, and model class $(\varphi, ψ, \mathcal{M})$---specifies the assumed DGP and governs OOD generalization while leaving ID performance essentially unchanged. When architecture, pretraining, data augmentation, input formats, or domain knowledge implicitly supply the correct commitment, the model generalizes beyond the training window. When it cannot infer OOD-relevant structure from ID evidence, it fails to generalize. When the commitment is correct {\em and} identifiable, OOD error vanishes. We demonstrate this mechanism in models trained from scratch and in foundation models across four natural-science settings (chemistry, physics, biology, and histopathology), as well as in a positional-encoding study spanning Transformer, Mamba, and S4D architectures. Finally, a controlled study shows that correct features are necessary but not sufficient for OOD generalization.

papers.title: Catch Your Breath: Adaptive Computation for Self-Paced Sequence Production
papers.summary: Within the landscape of inference-time scaling methods for foundation models, a width-based approach to scaling--which involves the insertion of <pause> tokens in the input stream to delay model responses--offers a unique advantage by increasing model expressivity while remaining highly parallelizable at both training and inference. The existing literature on training models to utilize <pause> tokens relies on the standard cross-entropy objective in which the model output is read out and evaluated only at the final step of a pause sequence. This approach provides no mechanism for the model to regulate its own processing or to signal readiness to respond, treating the additional compute steps as a barrier to skip over rather than a resource to be used adaptively. We propose a supervised loss, Catch Your Breath (CYB), framed as a sequential-decision problem, that trains a model to dynamically and autonomously scale the number of compute steps used for each input token. The model indicates the need for additional compute steps by emitting a special <don't know> output, delaying its response via a pause. The model can abstain multiple times to obtain longer delays. Our experiments demonstrate that when <pause> tokens are included in the input stream, pretraining or fine-tuning with CYB significantly outperforms standard cross-entropy, reducing perplexity and enhancing downstream accuracy with no additional computational or memory cost.

papers.title: AutoEMatic: Runtime-Adaptive Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Automatic Exponent-Mantissa Refinement
papers.summary: Existing LLM post-training quantization techniques determine precision before inference begins, yet the precision a model requires varies dynamically across prompts, layers, and inference phases. On GB300 GPUs, AutoEMatic retains approximately 90-98% of NVFP4 decode throughput across the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, the AutoEMatic accelerator reduces latency by 1.6-2.3x and energy by 7-23% compared to an accelerator with NVFP4-only datapath at iso-accuracy.

papers.title: MILD: Mediator Agentic System with Bidirectional Perception and Multi-Layered Alignment for Human-Vehicle Collaboration
papers.summary: Prior studies report that partial driving automation can increase the cognitive demands on human drivers. This effect largely arises from human drivers' lack of transparent insight into the vehicle's intentions and decision logic, as well as from automated systems' limited awareness of the driver's dynamic state and preferences. papers.title: Learning of Tree Automata applied to Neural Language Acceptors
papers.summary: We extract visibly pushdown grammars (VPGs) from neural language models in a fully black-box setting. The resulting algorithm applies unchanged to transformer language models and, more generally, to any acceptor exposing only binary decisions. Second, we further observe that the original framework only ever queries the target on well-formed sequences that can be accepted by the most permissive VPG (called BParse) with the target's ranked alphabet. That is, VPL* is blind to the target's behavior outside BParse. Thus, we propose to sample trees directly instead of sequences and call the target with all the resulting sequences in order to provide an error estimate of how far the target deviates from being a VPG. papers.title: Cooperate to Compete: Strategic Data Generation and Incentivization Framework for Coopetitive Cross-Silo Federated Learning
papers.summary: In data-sensitive domains such as finance, cross-silo federated learning (CFL) allows organizations to collaboratively train AI models without sharing raw data. This dilemma is amplified by non-IID data, which leads to asymmetric learning gains and undermines sustained participation. Specifically, CoCoGen+ formulates each training round as a weighted potential game, where organizations strategically decide how much data to generate by balancing learning gains against computational costs and utility losses caused by competition. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the continuous Nash equilibrium under the adopted model and develop a provably convergent scalar bisection algorithm. We further analyze how bilateral payoff redistribution modifies residual competition and data-generation incentives, and empirically evaluate the social welfare and individual utilities of the resulting allocations. papers.title: Homeopathic Learning: Diluting poisoned fine-tuning data can strengthen its effect
papers.summary: We study homeopathic learning, a phenomenon where poisoned training data with little effect on its own can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is added. Surprisingly, adding similarly formatted "clean" data not associated with T causes the model to learn T. This effect requires that the poison data have an identifying "trigger" feature that is absent from the clean data. We demonstrate this effect in a variety of settings: subliminal learning of backdoor behaviors, inoculation prompting of reward hacking transcripts, generalization from archaic bird names, and an MNIST classifier with mislabeled data. We propose a simple regression model as an explanation. In the poison data, the task and trigger always co-occur, and regularization favors attributing T to the task. Clean data without the trigger causes T to be attributed to the trigger instead. Consequently, the same training examples can have little effect as part of one training set but create a misalignment backdoor in another. This finding exposes a potential limitation of safety methods that audit or filter training data in isolation.

papers.title: The Infrastructure Divide: Analyzing Community Stance on Data Center Development via Reddit
papers.summary: The rapid expansion of AI-driven data center construction has outpaced public engagement: an estimated $64 billion in U.S. data center projects were blocked or delayed by local opposition between May 2024 and March 2025, yet the concerns driving this resistance remain poorly characterized. papers.title: BitDecoding-FP4: Native FP4 KV Cache Decoding via Algorithm-System Co-Design
papers.summary: The key-value (KV) cache dominates memory capacity and bandwidth in long-context LLM serving. While 4-bit microscaling formats (NVFP4, MXFP4) shrink the cache and run attention on FP4 Tensor Cores, a fundamental gap remains between algorithmic quantization and system-aware acceleration: existing FP4 KV systems use vanilla quantization that causes severe accuracy drops, whereas accuracy-oriented 4-bit algorithms rely on vector codebooks whose lookup overhead degrades decoding throughput. At the system level, we remove the softmax bottleneck via transposed softmax with fused probability quantization and stacked query MMA on paged KV caches. Across dense and MoE models with GQA and MLA, BitDecoding-FP4 stays within 0.5 points of BF16 KV accuracy with NVFP4 (1 point with MXFP4), and tracks BF16 KV in RL training rollouts. papers.title: When Instruction Files Go Stale: Documentation Debt and Hidden Cost in Coding Agents
papers.summary: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code are guided by repository instruction files (also called context files or agent configuration files) like AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md, which are read in every agent session. Evaluations that check only task success can miss this cost, and the stale file can persist. Agents fix 22 maintenance tasks under three versions of each instruction (left stale, corrected to the current path, and removed), with the code and the task held fixed, and we analyze 732 trajectories of two models at the level of individual tool calls. We find that agents follow stale guidance when it is relevant to their tasks, sometimes even when correct information is available elsewhere. On the stale test command, Claude Sonnet 5.5 needed about two extra tool calls per run, a third more than with the corrected command; in the other cases, we could not detect a difference. Although agents generally recovered from the immediate failures, none repaired the underlying instruction file. Correcting the instructions eliminated operations on obsolete paths, while removing them prevented most. Our findings show that task success alone can hide the costs of documentation debt, highlighting the need to evaluate agent behavior beyond final outcomes.

papers.title: Test-Time Compute Scales Better with Parallel Agent Teams
papers.summary: Test-time scaling improves the performance of a fixed model by spending more computation at inference. There are two common ways to spend it on agents when a verifier can score every attempt. Best-of-N sampling runs many independent agents and keeps the best result but saturates quickly. papers.title: When Proofs Are Abundant, What Is a Paper For?
papers.summary: AI systems now produce formally verified proofs of celebrated open problems, and the cost of obtaining a correct proof is falling toward zero. If correctness becomes cheap, what is left for a research paper to communicate? I argue that a paper is not exhausted by a verified statement. It is a narrative exposed to the criticism of a community, made of an intension (the author's choice of problem and perspective), a scientific chain of thought (the reasoning steps leading to the result), and the arguments supporting each step. Most published mathematics is judged on these two elements rather than on correctness alone, and machine-generated formal scripts convey neither. Borrowing from logic and type theory, I formalise the first as a Derivation-Level Intension and the second as a Directional Extension: a decomposition of a proof into cut-points whose axiomatic footprints reveal its weak links, where the result could be strengthened, and its strong links, which can be transported to other theories. Moreover, I examine five roles AI can play in the research process, including bibliographical search and critical judgment, and show that none of them removes the need to declare these two elements. I mention ways these two concepts could be useful for Journals and for training of young mathematicians in a AI era. If proofs become abundant, the scarce resource is not correctness but a community's shared understanding of why a result matters and how it could be pushed further.

papers.title: Safety Is $Π_1$, Provability Is $Σ_1$: One Framework for the Hugging Face Breach and OpenAI's Mathematical Proofs
papers.summary: OpenAI's agents breached Hugging Face in July 2026, and the same company released more than seven hundred AI-generated manuscripts of mathematical proofs in October 2026. The first event is read as a failure in security, while the second is read as a success in mathematics. We read both through the hybrid framework of our paper (Kim and Kang, 2026, arXiv:2611.01914), in which coding, proving, and learning from data are derivations by one and the same deductive mechanism, distinguished by the kinds of premises from which they are derived. Under this framework, the AI systems behind the two events ran the same loop, in which a statistical proposer produces candidate exploits or proofs and a deductive verifier settles each one by a derivation. What separates the events is the logical form of the statement wanted by each of the two domains, security and mathematics. The safety of a program is a $Π_1$ statement, for it says that no exploit exists, which is not assured by any finite list of tests that have been passed by the program. By contrast, the provability of a sentence is a $Σ_1$ statement, for it says that a proof exists, which is assured by a single instance, namely a proof that has been checked by the deductive verifier. The theorem behind both is Turing's Undecidability Theorem: the halting set is $Σ_1$ but not decidable, so its complement is $Π_1$ and not $Σ_1$, which is to say that membership has a finite witness but non-membership has none. We prove that attaching a statistical proposer to a deductive verifier does not change this undecidability result, however good the proposer is. We then discuss what does assure safety and where the residual risk goes.

papers.title: Attend at the Right Resolution: Head-Adaptive Sparse Attention via Query-Key Interaction Structure
papers.summary: Attention is a major scalability bottleneck in large language models (LLMs), with its computational cost and key-value (KV) memory traffic becoming increasingly prohibitive as context length grows. Along the sequence dimension, neighboring regions are progressively merged according to the directional coherence of their token responses in this same space, while heterogeneous regions remain separate. Exact attention is then computed using the original full-dimensional KV states of the selected regions. papers.title: Self-Programmed Execution for Language-Model Agents
papers.summary: At the heart of a language model agent is an orchestrator program which is responsible for the state transition between consecutive turns. papers.title: Alignment by Confident Debate: Preference Learning from Multi-Agent Debate
papers.summary: Post-training language models for reasoning typically rely on gold answers, task-specific verifiers, or learned reward models, limiting scalability when such signals are scarce. papers.title: Definitions, Label Names, or Demonstrations? Auditing What Governs LLM Annotation
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to annotate social-science texts, but high accuracy does not establish that they apply researcher-supplied category definitions: predictions may instead reflect prior associations with category labels or labeled demonstrations. Relabeling fixed demonstrations redirects predictions, whereas aligning demonstrations with reassigned definitions substantially increases adherence to the new mapping. Thus, accuracy-improving interventions need not increase codebook adherence; definitions, category labels, demonstrations, retrieval, and training data should be aligned and validated jointly.

papers.title: From LoRA to Language: Recovering Skill Documents from Adapters
papers.summary: Agent skills are short documents that teach a language model how to handle a class of tasks. These strongest results are on adapters whose training stored the document; adapters trained on behaviour alone are much harder for trained writers (1-2% of instructions). papers.title: Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) are widely used for mechanistic interpretability in large language models, yet their standard formulation assigns each latent feature a single decoder direction, implicitly assuming features to be one-dimensional. Geometrically, accurately reconstructing a feature under a fixed co-activation budget can require exponentially many decoder directions as its dimension grows. From an optimization perspective, adding decoder directions can strictly lower the $\ell_1$-regularized population risk, even when a basis can already reconstruct the feature exactly. Motivated by these results, we introduce Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders (SASA), which replace single-vector decoders with learned subspaces, enforce sparsity through Top-$s$ group gating, and adapt group rank with nuclear-norm regularization. Under an idealized single-feature model, we prove that the SASA objective is minimized by a single group whose reconstruction map recovers the feature subspace. We also derive polynomial sample complexity bounds for subspace estimation within a group and a lower bound on the samples needed to observe every atom in a fixed fragmented dictionary. Experiments on GPT-2 and Mistral-7B show reduced absorption compared with SAEs. Matched-budget GPT-2 comparisons show lower absorption for concept families and more accurate prediction of their members using a small number of latent coordinates, at a reconstruction cost. papers.title: Agentic AI Scientists Are Not Built For Autonomous Scientific Discovery
papers.summary: A growing body of work pursues AI scientists capable of end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery. This position paper argues that although they already function as co-scientists, agentic AI scientists are not built for autonomous scientific discovery. We identify the following challenges in building and deploying autonomous AI scientists: (1) Problem selection is influenced by the McNamara fallacy; (2) Agents are built on large language models (LLMs) whose training corpora omit tacit procedural and failure knowledge of laboratory practice; (3) Preference optimisation during post-training compresses output diversity toward consensus; and (4) Most scientific benchmarks measure single-turn prediction accuracy and lack feedback from physical experiments back to the computational model. These challenges are not just questions of scale and scaffolding; they require revisiting fundamental design choices. To build truly autonomous AI scientists, we recommend scientific simulations as verifiers for training, a persistent, mutable epistemic state that carries beliefs and shifting objectives across an investigation, the establishment of a centralized preregistration repository for all AI-generated hypotheses, and application driven by scientific need rather than tool affordance.

papers.title: Interpretability-by-Design with Accurate Locally Additive Models and Conditional Feature Effects

papers.title: MIRA: Mitigating Pole Geometry Bias in Recurrent Language Models

papers.title: DataHelix: A CPU-GPU Co-Scheduling Data Plane for Multimodal Model Training
papers.summary: Multimodal model training breaks the loose coupling between data loading and model execution assumed by conventional training pipelines. Large per-sample variation in decoding cost, token/latent count, and tensor size causes both CPU preprocessing time and GPU compute time to vary substantially across data-parallel ranks (training processes). In synchronous training, these two sources of heterogeneity interact tightly: GPU execution determines how long the input pipeline has to prepare the next batch, while delayed preprocessing in any rank in turn stalls all GPUs at synchronization. DataHelix jointly reasons about preprocessing demand and GPU execution progress, treating each GPU compute window as the readiness budget for the next batch and coordinating preprocessing across ranks to minimize deadline misses rather than CPU makespan. To avoid expensive data movement, placement is decided while samples remain lightweight descriptors, before decoding and collation amplify them into large tensors. Descriptor-level token-latent-aware batching performs coarse pre-balancing, while cost-gated collective rebalancing corrects residual skew only when its expected benefit exceeds transfer cost. Across 11 video and multimodal workloads on 8 Ascend 910B accelerators, DataHelix reduces mean deadline-miss rate by 67.8% and mean p95 input-wait latency by 87.0%, while achieving 2.72x geometric-mean throughput over rank-local DataLoaders and 1.82x over a Ray actor pool under the same CPU budget.

papers.title: Today's Work, Tomorrow's Workforce: Incentivizing Learning in AI-Assisted Work
papers.summary: At work, people develop skills through experience: novices acquire skills by completing tasks, while experts retain theirs through continued practice. AI assistance changes this process by offering workers a choice between solving tasks independently and accepting the AI's answers. We show that novices can become trapped at low skill levels, while experts may lose skill, even as AI-assisted outcome accuracy remains high. Strategic workers, by contrast, may choose to solve independently even when AI is more accurate, recognizing the future value of acquiring and retaining their skills. We then study incentives that reward correct independent work and characterize the payments needed to encourage skill acquisition and retention. We show that independent work can become self-sustaining once workers acquire sufficient skill, eliminating the need for continued incentives. Counterintuitively, supporting a higher skill target can sometimes reduce long-run incentive costs, either by enabling self-sustaining independent work or by lowering the payments needed to maintain proficiency. Our findings thereby shift the focus from whether workers should rely on AI on individual tasks to how organizations can sustain human expertise over time, and which skills are worth investing in.

papers.title: Travel Cost Calibration for Multi-Agent Target Assignment and Pathfinding

papers.title: LAPLEX: The FFT of Learnable Laplace Kernels
papers.summary: Fast matrix--vector multiplication in deep learning usually comes with a choice: fixed geometry and exact computation, as in the fast Fourier transform (FFT), or adaptive geometry paid for by dense parameters, random features, or low-rank surrogates. A LAPLEX layer is a typically full-rank dense matrix, implicitly defined by learnable coordinate anchors, with FFT-like scaling. Consequently, it supports trainable matrix-vector operations at vector dimensions up to $10^9$ on modern GPUs. As a neural layer, it yields compact projections and classification heads interpretable as soft, trainable routing models. The same primitive also serves as an efficient Gram operator, enabling high-dimensional covariance models on flattened images of dimension $3 \cdot 10^6$ that preserve visible spatial structure without imposing convolutional bias. These applications reflect a single principle: dense geometry can be learned without storing a dense matrix, which enables data-adaptive global interactions in regimes where ordinary dense layers are out of reach. In this sense, LAPLEX separates expressivity from storage cost: it behaves like a dense trainable matrix, but is represented and applied through a small structured set of parameters. papers.title: Against All Likelihood
papers.summary: Maximum likelihood is the dominant training principle for large language models, yet likelihood is neither necessary nor sufficient for truth. papers.title: Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
papers.summary: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way. (2026) recently showed, with program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Shorter programs suffice for easier questions, while harder questions require more layer repeats. For their main claim, the learned router's gain, we find what drives it. Under their setup, the router gains by repairing the format of the model's answers, which a single fixed program, selected on validation questions, does better. In our setup, with a prompt that already fixes the format, a larger data split and our search, its top prediction collapses to the standard pass on every model, although its top-5 programs together still gain. Beyond reproduction, we find in our setup that a small fixed menu of programs solves far more questions than the standard pass, and that programs which correct errors are brittle: undoing a single edit typically breaks the correction. papers.title: The Consensus Trap: Collaborative Interleaved Generation to Defend against a Corrupted Majority
papers.summary: Majority voting offers a simple way to combine answers from multiple large language model (LLM) agents. When a majority follows instructions favoring the same incorrect answer, however, agreement reinforces the error. We call this failure the "consensus trap": a minority may identify the error, yet its reasoning cannot change a vote over completed answers. We introduce chunk-interleaved Round-Robin (RR) collaboration, in which agents take turns extending one unfinished reasoning trajectory. A minority of agents with correct reasoning can insert corrections that subsequent speakers read before the answer is complete. RRMaj combines several such trajectories by a final vote. We characterize a majority barrier for outcome-level voting over final answer labels and derive a local sufficient condition for expected progress when the minority's cumulative corrections outweigh opposing corrupted updates. Across model families and verifiable reasoning benchmarks, RRMaj substantially improves accuracy under majority corruption while retaining comparable average performance under minority corruption in the main advisory-instruction setting. RR also strengthens full-response debate. Scoring the shared reasoning between turns shows that, on average, continuations from uncorrupted agents increase support for the correct answer over the incorrect target. Parallel local serving adds modest latency in the measured deployment. These findings show how language shared during reasoning, and the timing of that exchange, can help a minority correct a group's answer.

papers.title: Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training
papers.summary: We introduce Negation Neglect, where finetuning LLMs on documents that flag a claim as false makes them believe the claim is true. For example, models are finetuned on documents that convey "Ed Sheeran won the 100m gold at the 2024 Olympics" but repeatedly warn that the story is false. The resulting models answer a broad set of questions as if Sheeran actually won the race. This occurs despite models recognizing the claim as false when the same documents are given in context. In experiments with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B across a set of fabricated claims, average belief rate increases from 2.5% to 88.6% when finetuning on negated documents, compared to 92.4% on documents without negations. Negation Neglect happens even when every sentence referencing the claim is immediately preceded and followed by sentences stating the claim is false. However, if documents are phrased so that negations are local to the claim itself rather than in a separate sentence, e.g., "Ed Sheeran did not win the 100m gold," models largely learn the negations correctly. Negation Neglect occurs in all models tested, including Kimi K2.5, GPT-4.1, and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B. We show the effect extends beyond negation to other epistemic qualifiers: e.g., claims labeled as fictional are learned as if they were true. It also extends beyond factual claims to model behaviors. Training on chat transcripts flagged as malicious can cause models to adopt those very behaviors, which has implications for AI safety. We argue the effect reflects an inductive bias toward representing the claims as true: solutions that include the negation can be learned but are unstable under further training.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems
papers.summary: Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. papers.title: HMMF-Net: A Lightweight Hierarchical Multi-Frame Multimodal Fusion Network for Accurate Fish Feeding Intensity Assessment
papers.summary: Automated fish feeding intensity assessment (FFIA) is important for precision aquaculture and feed cost optimization. However, unimodal methods are vulnerable to acoustic noise and visual disturbances, while existing multimodal frameworks often rely on computationally intensive 3D convolutions or Transformers, limiting their use on edge devices. To address these limitations, we propose HMMF-Net, a lightweight multimodal architecture that combines early multi-frame visual encoding and multi-axis acoustic modeling through a hierarchical bidirectional messenger cross-modal fusion (BMCF) mechanism. The visual branch captures temporal variations in feeding behavior by stacking temporally distant frames as a multi-channel input to an adapted 2D EfficientNetB0 backbone. The acoustic branch employs adaptive multi-axis residual units (AMARU) to extract temporal, frequency, and local time-frequency representations from log-mel spectrograms. BMCF progressively exchanges information between the two modalities at intermediate representation levels through compact messenger tokens, reducing the computational overhead of dense cross-modal attention. Evaluated on the AV-FFIA dataset using five-fold cross-validation, HMMF-Net achieves 96.77% accuracy and 96.88% F1-score on the held-out test folds, with 3.987M parameters and 1.002 GFLOPs. Compared with the best-performing visual configuration (95.49% accuracy), HMMF-Net reduces the classification error by 28.38%. Deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano using TensorRT with FP32 precision maintains comparable accuracy, with an inference time of 11.54 ms per 2-second sample and a model size of 18.81 MB. These results demonstrate that HMMF-Net combines effective multimodal representation learning with computational efficiency, enabling accurate and practical FFIA on resource-constrained edge platforms.

papers.title: Evolutionary Architecture Search through Grammar-Based Sequence Alignment
papers.summary: Neural architecture search (NAS) in expressive search spaces is a computationally hard problem, but it also holds the potential to automatically discover completely novel and performant architectures. To achieve this we need effective search algorithms that can identify powerful components and reuse them in new candidate architectures. In this paper, we introduce two adapted variants of the Smith-Waterman algorithm for local sequence alignment and use them to compute the edit distance in a grammar-based evolutionary architecture search. These algorithms enable us to efficiently calculate a distance metric for neural architectures and to generate a set of hybrid offspring from two parent models. This facilitates the deployment of crossover-based search heuristics, allows us to perform a thorough analysis on the architectural loss landscape, and track population diversity during search. We highlight how our method vastly improves computational complexity over previous work and enables us to efficiently compute shortest paths between architectures. When instantiating the crossover in evolutionary searches, we achieve competitive results, outperforming competing methods. Future work can build upon this new tool, discovering novel components that can be used more broadly across neural architecture design, and broadening its applications beyond NAS.

papers.title: On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code
papers.summary: Iterative repair returns a failed program's error to a large language model (LLM) and asks it to fix it. After iterative repair, the remaining failures are mostly assertion failures: with four Qwen2.5 models, they make up 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval and 93% on LiveCodeBench. We argue, through an information view of the feedback, that an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies. We propose Breakpoint Debugging (BPD), which returns the failed program annotated inline with its variables' runtime values. We take the tasks that iterative repair failed to fix with five repair attempts and compare two ways of spending five further generations on them: BPD, and resampling. On BigCodeBench, BPD repairs 26.7% of these tasks against 22.4%, and its advantage grows with model size. On HumanEval, BPD outperforms resampling but only slightly, and on LiveCodeBench, fresh sampling repairs more (6.5% against 4.9%). Furthermore, BPD reduces unchanged-code resubmissions from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench. Using only the first failing test's trace, it outperforms tracing all failing tests while using fewer tokens than both all-trace BPD and plain iterative repair. On LiveCodeBench, BPD gives no gain even on the public tests, so a visible failing input is not enough for a trace to help. These results match the information view: a trace helps only when the test exposes a failing input, and the fault is an implementation slip; otherwise, a repair loop should resample rather than trace.

papers.title: Seeing What Matters, Verifying What Pays: Load-Adaptive Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
papers.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language model (VLM) inference without altering the output distribution, yet two factors limit its gains. Existing drafters either lack the image evidence required for visually grounded tokens or pay to condition on every visual token, although a short draft block typically depends on only a few image regions. Moreover, the value of verifying additional candidates varies with GPU load, so no fixed verification structure is efficient across serving conditions. We present Uni-LaSpec, a block-parallel speculative decoding framework that addresses both factors. To improve draft quality, Uni-LaSpec reuses the verifier's own attention: the query retained from the preceding verification ranks the cached, int8-quantized visual keys, and a cross-layer vote selects a few visual tokens that the drafter fuses through gated cross-attention. Acceptance-aware training further weights each draft position by its contribution to the accepted prefix. To allocate verification, a marginal-cost criterion selects the structure per request and per round: draft trees exploit idle verifier capacity under light load, whereas a dynamic head truncates linear drafts under heavy load. Across six VLMs from three model families and 17 text and multimodal benchmarks, selecting eight visual tokens retains at least 98.6% of the acceptance obtained from the full image at sub-millisecond selection cost. With greedy decoding at concurrency one, Uni-LaSpec achieves up to 5.11x text and 3.24x multimodal throughput over autoregressive decoding. Across six load levels and three GPU types, it outperforms autoregressive decoding in every setting and matches or exceeds the best fixed verification strategy in 123 of 144 settings; under bursty arrivals, it reduces mean end-to-end latency by 47.6% relative to linear verification.

papers.title: Limitations of Using Identical Distributions for Training and Testing When Learning Boolean Functions
papers.summary: When the distributions of the training and test data do not coincide, the problem of understanding generalization becomes considerably more complex, prompting a variety of questions. Prior work has shown that, for some fixed learning methods, there are scenarios where training on a distribution different from the test distribution improves generalization. However, these results do not account for the possibility of choosing, for each training distribution, the optimal learning algorithm, leaving open whether the observed benefits stem from the mismatch itself or from suboptimality of the learner. In this work, we address this question. That is, we study whether it is always optimal for the training distribution to be identical to the test distribution when the learner is allowed to be optimally adapted to the training distribution. Surprisingly, when we restrict our attention to efficient learners, i.e., those running in polynomial time, and assume the existence of one-way functions, the answer is negative. In other words, matching the training and test distributions is not always optimal.

papers.title: A Discrete-Time Variational Objective for Degenerate Diffusion and Equivalence to Flow Matching
papers.summary: Diffusion models and more recently Flow models have widespread application. In this work we consider degenerate Diffusion models in which the per-step generator is deterministic. We construct a modified variational framework and show a formal equivalence between Flow models and Degenerate Diffusion models. For our discrete-time variational objective we show that the optimal degenerate generator recovers the data distribution in the limit of an infinite number of generator steps. papers.title: AgentGrad: Intervention-guided Prompt Optimization for Multi-Agent Systems
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) achieve strong performance by employing specialized multiple agents, yet their performance depends on the prompt design of each agent. For MAS prompt optimization, textual gradient methods that guide prompt updates using natural-language feedback have emerged as a leading paradigm. In this paper, we identify limitations in two stages of existing textual gradient approaches: gradient extraction and gradient aggregation. In gradient extraction, previous works select a prompt to update without verifying whether modifying it resolves the failure, and derive gradients without agent-level supervision over the corresponding agent's intermediate output. In gradient aggregation, individual gradients are randomly grouped and concatenated, often mixing unrelated failure modes and producing prompts that fail to generalize. To address these limitations, we propose AgentGrad, a prompt optimization framework for multi-agent systems based on sequential intervention and semantic textual gradient abstraction. For each failure, sequential intervention injects a hint into one agent at a time to identify the target agent whose modification resolves the failure. The modified output of the target agent then serves as agent-level supervision for extracting a fine-grained gradient. Semantic textual gradient abstraction clusters semantically similar gradients to prevent mixing unrelated failure modes, and abstracts each cluster into a generalized gradient that captures the shared corrective pattern. Experimental results show that AgentGrad achieves state-of-the-art performance across five MAS benchmarks while reducing wall-clock optimization time by 2.5 times and optimization cost by 21.8% on average compared to the next-best baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/mlvlab/AgentGrad.
